correctness.rationale: The exact full-Cayley receive-ball intersection criterion is Kendall distance at most two. The orientation-sign argument proves a sharp all-length lower bound and the local-DAG construction achieves it. Distinct same-orientation words have distance at least three. For n=1..7 all zigzag words and collisions were exhaustively generated, each small component independent-set count was exhausted, and at n=6 and 7 each conflict component was verified to be an isolated edge. A separate direct Kendall inversion-distance implementation agrees, and supplied attaining codebooks of 80 and 502 words are checked. The finite tests are explicitly separated from the all-n proof.

originality.rationale: The relevant primary full texts and published closest claims were inspected and compared by implication. Existing unrestricted Kendall permutation code bounds and equality censuses do not give the two zigzag orientation source capacity or its finite optimal-codebook multiplicity. A fixed-fence linear-extension exchange theorem differs in both graph and objective; the other alternating-permutation result uses permutation parity, not zigzag signs. Exact cross-orientation minimum and 42-edge plateau were not found in actually searched records. Residual priority uncertainty is retained.
residual_risks: Equivalent results in obscure or unindexed previous literature cannot be excluded by a finite search.
Published secondary database catalogues may have omitted exact finite enumerations; absence in searches is not proof of novelty.

value.rationale: Up-down permutations form a classical Euler-counted constrained rank-modulation alphabet. The code-design question of when the complete constrained source corrects one local error is natural and admits a sharp all-n answer: length eight. The constructive orientation distance theorem explains the transition. Exact 42-edge equal ambiguity at two successive lengths, 80/502 capacity and 2^42 optimal dictionaries yield useful structural finite benchmarks, not a routine substitution or merely a small numerical improvement.
